lead: This unit turns VR and AR ideas into working 3D interaction: how users select, move, travel and command; how toolkits and engines build scenes; how C# scripts add interaction and physics; and how to keep users safe and evaluate interfaces. After it you can choose interaction techniques, build a small Unity VR scene with physics, and run a simple usability test.
about: Unit 5 connects user action to VR development. Chapter 5.1 covers manipulation tasks and techniques; 5.2 travel and wayfinding; 5.3 system control by menus, voice and gesture. 5.4 explains VR toolkits and scene graphs, which 5.5 uses to compare Unity and Unreal. 5.6 adds C# scripting, collisions and physics. 5.7 then covers human factors and safety, and 5.8 closes with usability guidelines and evaluation. The order moves from what the user does, to how software represents and runs the world, to how we test and protect the user.

chapters.idea: 3D manipulation lets a user select an object and change its position, orientation or size with a chosen technique and constraint.
chapters.depth: Selection, positioning, rotation and scaling; one, two and six degree-of-freedom (6 DOF) tasks; constraints and snap. Techniques: direct virtual hand, ray casting, Go-Go, HOMER, world-in-miniature, props and haptic handles. Input device choice links to Unit 2. Design guidelines: feedback, gain, threshold, fatigue, two-handed manipulation. Some syllabi call this 3D manipulation or direct manipulation.

figure.title: Manipulation loop
figure.aria: A five-step flow: select an object, choose a transform, apply a manipulation technique, constrain the motion, then confirm.

chapters.example: A controller ray starts at (0, 0, 0) and points along (0, 0, −1). A sphere has centre (0.10, 0, −2.00) m and radius 0.15 m. Find the perpendicular distance from the ray to the centre and say whether the ray selects the sphere.
chapters.trap: Ray selection is not based on distance alone; a ray can point past a near object and still miss if the perpendicular distance to the object centre is larger than its radius.
chapters.leave: Input hardware detail to Unit 2; shading and rendering to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Travel moves the viewpoint through the virtual world, while wayfinding helps the user know where to go and stay oriented.
chapters.depth: Travel tasks: exploration, search, manoeuvring. Techniques: physical walking, steering, fly, gaze-directed, point-and-go, teleport, world scaling. Wayfinding: theoretical foundations (landmarks, route and survey knowledge), user-centred support (maps, signs, guides), environment-centred support (lighting, layout, landmarks), evaluating aids, design guidelines. Some syllabi call this navigation and wayfinding.

figure.aria: A map graph with Start at (0,0), East at (3,0) and Final at (3,4); the walked route is 3 m then 4 m, while the dashed straight-line distance is 5 m.

chapters.example: A virtual campus has the user at (0, 0) m on a map. The user walks 3 m east, then 4 m north. Compute the straight-line distance from start to final point and compare it with the route length.
chapters.trap: Route length is not straight-line distance; wayfinding aids may shorten perceived effort but not the physical path.
chapters.leave: Tracker mathematics to Unit 2; 3D sound to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: System control changes the application itself, not a scene object, through menus, voice, gesture or a mix of these.
chapters.depth: Classification of system control; graphical menus (2D, 3D, pie, marking menus); voice commands (grammar, confirmation, error recovery); gestural commands (pose and motion, delimiting); tools; multimodal system control and fusion. Design guidelines: mode, feedback, discoverability, false activation. Some syllabi call this command and control.
chapters.example: An app accepts voice and gesture. In 100 commands, 70 are voice, 20 gesture and 10 menu. Voice succeeds 90% of its commands, gesture 80%, menu 100%. Compute total successful commands and overall success rate.
chapters.trap: Do not average success percentages across unequal command counts; weight by the number of commands.
chapters.leave: Speech recognition internals and AR marker commands to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A scene graph is a tree that stores the virtual world as nodes with transforms, geometry and state, so a toolkit can traverse and draw it efficiently.
chapters.depth: Scene graph as a tree of nodes: group, transform, geometry, material, camera, light. Local and world transforms, traversal order, retained mode, state changes, bounding volumes and culling. Toolkits: Unity scene and prefab model; Unreal level and actor model; OpenSceneGraph; historical VRML and X3D. Some syllabi call this scene graph or retained-mode graphics. Only a few universities teach X3D in detail.
chapters.example: A scene graph has root S with child T (translate 2 m on x) and child M under T (translate 3 m on x). A point is at (1, 0, 0) m in the local frame of M. Compute its world x.
chapters.trap: Parent transforms apply before child transforms; adding local and world coordinates in the wrong order gives the wrong position.
chapters.leave: Rendering pipeline to Unit 4; AR SDK details to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Unity and Unreal are game engines that provide an editor, scene model, asset pipeline, lighting and build path for VR and AR applications.
chapters.depth: Unity: editor, GameObject, Component, Prefab, Scene, Asset Store; C# scripts. Unreal: Actor, Component, Level, Blueprint; C++ where needed. Import models from Maya, 3ds Max and Blender; apply materials, textures, lighting and shading; camera projection types; build to headset or phone. Compare workflow, asset pipeline and performance. Some syllabi call this game engine development.

figure.title: Engine workflow
figure.aria: A left-to-right engine workflow: import an asset, build the scene, attach scripts, bake lighting and build to the device.

chapters.example: A Unity scene has 60 cubes in 3 materials, 20 cubes per material. A batch holds at most 15 cubes of one material. Find the number of draw calls with perfect batching and with no batching.
chapters.trap: Draw calls are not one per object when batching works; batching needs shared material and compatible state.
chapters.leave: Modeling theory to Unit 4; AR tracking SDKs to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: C# scripts connect input, interaction logic and the physics engine, so objects move and react under rules rather than by animation alone.
chapters.depth: MonoBehaviour lifecycle: Awake, Start, Update, FixedUpdate, OnTriggerEnter. Input polling, events, coroutines, raycasts, layers. Rigidbody, collider, trigger, joint, force, impulse, mass; collision detection and response. Haptic callbacks. Keep C# examples small. Some syllabi call this VR programming.

figure.aria: A sequence where input sends a button event to the script, the script calls AddForce on physics, physics returns a collision hit, and the script updates the display.

chapters.example: A Rigidbody cube of mass 0.8 kg starts from rest. A horizontal impulse of 1.6 N·s is applied. Find its speed just after the impulse and the distance it travels in the next 0.5 s with no friction.
chapters.trap: Impulse is force times time, not force; use FixedUpdate for physics and keep units in N, kg and m/s.
chapters.leave: Shader code to Unit 4; networked physics is not covered.

chapters.idea: VR can make users uncomfortable or unsafe, so latency, display conflicts, hygiene and session limits must be designed and checked.
chapters.depth: Human factors: simulator sickness, cybersickness, latency, flicker, vergence-accommodation conflict, interpupillary distance, field of view, fatigue, hygiene, safety boundary, seated and standing use, breaks. Guidelines for session length, comfort, tracking loss and emergency stop. Some syllabi call this health and safety.

figure.aria: A 45-minute session timeline: 5 minutes setup, 15 minutes VR use, a 5-minute break, another 15 minutes VR use and 5 minutes rest.

chapters.example: A VR system has sensor delay 3 ms, simulation 6 ms, render 9 ms and display 2 ms. Compute motion-to-photon latency. Does it meet a 20 ms target?
chapters.trap: Motion-to-photon latency includes sensor, simulation, render and display; render time alone is not the full delay.
chapters.leave: Clinical diagnosis and treatment; display optics to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Usability evaluation checks whether a 3D interface is learnable, efficient and comfortable by measuring real user task performance and feedback.
chapters.depth: Usability guidelines for 3D interfaces: visibility, feedback, consistency, error prevention, user control, fatigue. Formative and summative evaluation; expert review, think-aloud, task-based test; metrics completion rate, error rate, task time, SUS, NASA-TLX, presence. A/B comparison. Some syllabi call this evaluation of 3D user interfaces.

figure.title: Success and error counts
figure.aria: A table of counts: design A has 16 of 20 users succeed and 6 of 40 attempts in error; design B has 18 of 20 succeed and 3 of 40 in error.

chapters.example: Two VR menu designs are tested by 20 users each. Design A: 16 users complete the task; 40 attempts contain 6 errors. Design B: 18 users complete; 40 attempts contain 3 errors. Compute completion rate and error rate for each.
chapters.trap: Completion rate uses users as denominator; error rate uses attempts; mixing them gives wrong metrics.
chapters.leave: Full statistical tests; presence theory to Unit 1.

links: scene graphs become Unity or Unreal scenes
interaction techniques are judged by usability tests
